1.note: The psalmist is speaking as if he were actually in a legal proceeding and wanted God to take his side, as if he were a judge who would **Vindicate** him or a defense attorney who would **plead** his case. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Recognize that I am innocent and defend me]

The psalmist is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. If you decide to retain the legal image in your translation, you may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and plead my case]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means all of the people who are acting in a **deceitful** and **unjust** way toward him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [from these deceitful and unjust people] or [from every deceitful and unjust person]

2.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **God** as being like a **refuge** for him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you are the God who is like a refuge to me]
See how you translated the term “refuge” in 11:1. Alternate translation: [you are the God who protects me]

2.q: לָ⁠מָ֪ה זְנַ֫חְתָּ֥⁠נִי לָֽ⁠מָּה־קֹדֵ֥ר אֶתְהַלֵּ֗ךְ בְּ⁠לַ֣חַץ אוֹיֵֽב
2.note: See how you translated the similar questions in 42:9. Alternate translation: [You appear to have rejected me! I should not have to walk about mourning because of the oppression of the enemy!]

For poetic effect, the psalmist is using again the same phrases that he used in 42:9. We recommend that you show this to your readers by translating the phrases here the same way that you translated them there. Alternate translation: [I should not have to go through life mourning because of the enemies who are oppressing me!]

While the psalmist uses essentially the same language here as in 42:9, he uses a different form of the verb translated as **walk**. The form used here can indicate repeated action, and that seems to be the sense in this context. Your language may have a comparable verbal form that you can use in your translation. If not, you may be able to use a different verb or expression. Alternate translation: [Why do I wander about]

3.note: The psalmist is speaking of God’s **light** and **truth** as if they were living things that God could **Send out** and that could **lead** the psalmist and **bring** him home. By **your light**, the psalmist probably means “the light of your face,” as in 4:6. This represents God’s favor, as if God were smiling and looking brightly at someone. By **faithfulness**, the psalmist probably means God’s covenant faithfulness, as in 42:8, that is, God’s commitment to fulfill the promises he has made to help people who are loyal to him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Extend your favor and faithfulness to me, and exhibit those qualities as you lead me. Exhibit those qualities in order to bring me]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **them** separately, even though the verb translated as **let them lead me** already includes this meaning. He is doing this because he is speaking of God’s **light** and **faithfulness** as if they were people and he wants to emphasize the personal role that he would like these qualities to take. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [let them be the ones who lead me]

The psalmist is not using the possessive form to ascribe **holiness** to the mountain where God’s **dwellings** are located. Instead, he is using the possessive form to indicate that God consecrated or set apart this mountain as a place where he would dwell, that is, where he would be present in a special way in his temple. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this purpose, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to the mountain that you have set apart] or [to the mountain that you have consecrated]

The psalmist is using the plural form **dwellings** where he could have used the singular form, since the context indicates that he is referring to the temple in Jerusalem (“the house of God,” 42:4, the location of “the altar of God,” 43:4). This suggests that he is using the plural form to emphasize the magnificence of the temple and especially its sacred character as a place where God is present in a special way. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the singular and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [your sacred temple]

4.note: The psalmist is speaking of God in the third person even though he is addressing him directly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person. Alternate translation: [to your altar, O God, to you, the God of the joy of my gladness]

The psalmist is using the possessive expression **the joy of my gladness** to describe **joy** that is characterized by **gladness**, that is, great joy. He is using the fuller possessive expression **the God of the joy of my gladness** to describe God as the one who gives him this great joy. If a speaker of your language would not use possessive forms for these purposes, you could express these ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [the God who gives me great joy]

5.q: מַה־תִּשְׁתּ֬וֹחֲחִ֨י ׀ נַפְשִׁ⁠י֮ וּֽ⁠מַה־תֶּהֱמִ֪י עָ֫לָ֥⁠י הוֹחִ֣ילִי לֵֽ֭⁠אלֹהִים כִּי־ע֣וֹד אוֹדֶ֑⁠נּוּ יְשׁוּעֹ֥ת פָּ֝נַ֗⁠י וֵֽ⁠אלֹהָֽ⁠י
5.note: This is the third occurrence of the refrain in this psalm. We recommend that you show this to your readers by translating the phrases here the same way that you translated them in the first two occurrences of this refrain in 42:5 and 42:11. Alternate translation: [I do not have to feel so despondent and agitated inside! I can hope in God. After all, I will again praise him, the one who saves me and who is my God]
